texts.orig: Q: What does it take to become a “senior” Product Manager?
texts.text: Q: What does it take to become a “senior” Product Manager?

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The PM career is unnecessarily shrouded in mystery. We all know you start as an individual contributor, and eventually, you can become a CPO or a VP of Product. But what happens in the middle? The answer is that you go through three milestones:
texts.text: The PM career is unnecessarily shrouded in mystery. We all know you start as an individual contributor, and eventually, you can become a CPO or a VP of Product. But what happens in the middle? The answer is that you go through three milestones:

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: You become a manager of PMs, usually called a Group PM, or Product Lead
texts.text: You become a manager of PMs, usually called a Group PM, or Product Lead

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: You become a manager of PM managers, usually called a Director
texts.text: You become a manager of PM managers, usually called a Director

texts.label: text
texts.orig: In my experience, of these three milestones, it takes the longest to progress through the first milestone, going from an entry-level PM to a senior PM. I’d guess that the median amount of time is 3 years, followed by 1-2 years to become a manager of PMs, and another 2-3 to become a Director.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: As an early-career PM, it can be hard to understand what it takes to become a “senior” PM, and how to get there. That’s because senior PMs don’t actually need to be much better than a regular PM at the kind of work a regular PM does. The biggest differences are behind the scenes.
texts.text: As an early-career PM, it can be hard to understand what it takes to become a “senior” PM, and how to get there. That’s because senior PMs don’t actually need to be much better than a regular PM at the kind of work a regular PM does. The biggest differences are behind the scenes.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Here’s an example, based on an interview question you’ll probably recognize:
texts.text: Here’s an example, based on an interview question you’ll probably recognize:

texts.label: text
texts.orig: A PM designs an alarm clock for the blind. They interview customers, test prototypes, and work closely with marketing to successfully launch the new product.
texts.text: A PM designs an alarm clock for the blind. They interview customers, test prototypes, and work closely with marketing to successfully launch the new product.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: A senior PM discovers the market opportunity for more accessible alarm clocks while speaking to customers and partners during their day-to-day work. They create a strategic plan to win the market, analyze which audience to address first, and convince executives to spin up a new team. Then, they interview customers, test prototypes, and work closely with marketing to successfully launch the new product.

texts.orig: A senior PM is responsible for developing and evangelizing a strategy that leads to meaningful customer and business success
texts.text: A senior PM is responsible for developing and evangelizing a strategy that leads to meaningful customer and business success

texts.label: text
texts.orig: They paint a picture of an inspiring future and figure out the best path to get there. They ensure that people understand the strategy and agree with it. They advocate for the resources they need, convincing executives to spin up the necessary teams.
texts.text: They paint a picture of an inspiring future and figure out the best path to get there. They ensure that people understand the strategy and agree with it. They advocate for the resources they need, convincing executives to spin up the necessary teams.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Newer PMs tend to prioritize work based on how much incremental value it adds to the product, while senior PMs prioritize work based on how much it moves the product towards the long term vision. For example, the top requested feature might be great for delighting the current customer base, but it could be more strategic to focus on features that expand the customer base.
texts.text: Newer PMs tend to prioritize work based on how much incremental value it adds to the product, while senior PMs prioritize work based on how much it moves the product towards the long term vision. For example, the top requested feature might be great for delighting the current customer base, but it could be more strategic to focus on features that expand the customer base.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: By focusing on strategy, senior PMs are able to reliably deliver great products that make a big impact for customers and the business.
texts.text: By focusing on strategy, senior PMs are able to reliably deliver great products that make a big impact for customers and the business.

texts.orig: Ironically, if you have a high level of autonomy it can be harder to earn trust. When you’re working independently, your manager won’t see all of the great decisions you make and the tough challenges you overcome. You’ll need to intentionally share your work with your manager.

texts.text: Luckily, there’s a template that helps avoid all these problems:

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: Hi manager, let me tell you about a challenge I ran into
texts.text: Hi manager, let me tell you about a challenge I ran into

texts.label: list_item

texts.label: text
texts.orig: This format lets you show off the challenge you faced and how you handled it, while also making an opening for feedback. If your solution was good, your manager can tell you, "Great work!" If there’s room for improvement, proactively asking for feedback at least demonstrates that you can be trusted to ask for input when you need it.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The more senior you get, the more you’ll be faced with decisions where the right answer is “it depends.”
texts.text: The more senior you get, the more you’ll be faced with decisions where the right answer is “it depends.”

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Senior PMs recognize these decisions and reason through them in a structured way. They can grapple with complex tradeoffs and ambiguous situations. They don’t fall back on rigid frameworks. They understand the goals and constraints of departments across the company and don't erroneously assume that their own team's goals are more important than those of any other team.
texts.text: Senior PMs recognize these decisions and reason through them in a structured way. They can grapple with complex tradeoffs and ambiguous situations. They don’t fall back on rigid frameworks. They understand the goals and constraints of departments across the company and don't erroneously assume that their own team's goals are more important than those of any other team.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: This doesn’t mean that it takes a senior PM days to make each decision. Due to their product expertise and rich mental models, they can lay out their thought process in minutes. Given an ambiguous problem area, they can rapidly pick out the most important problems to solve (and drive the work through to tangible impact).

Given an ambiguous problem area, they can rapidly pick out the most important problems to solve (and drive the work through to tangible impact).

texts.label: text
texts.orig: As a corollary to working on these nuanced problems, senior PMs also are expected to engage in constructive discussions with leaders at the company. They can effectively explain the nuance in the situation and the tradeoffs. They can defend their recommendation without becoming defensive.
texts.text: As a corollary to working on these nuanced problems, senior PMs also are expected to engage in constructive discussions with leaders at the company. They can effectively explain the nuance in the situation and the tradeoffs. They can defend their recommendation without becoming defensive.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: As you work on developing your nuanced thinking, the best guides are your teammates and stakeholders. Take their concerns seriously and look for the hidden complexity. What are the circumstances in which they’d be right? What information might they have that causes them to come to a different conclusion?

texts.label: text
texts.orig: As an example, imagine you’re launching a new feature and the head of customer support complains that it can’t be controlled by her team’s operational scripts. Instead of brushing her off and saying you'll update the scripts after launch, ask questions until you understand why she cares. You might learn that without the scripts it takes customer support representatives longer to answer tickets, which means customers will have a lower satisfaction rating, which correlates with them canceling their subscription. Once you see the broader implications, you might decide it's better to delay the launch until the scripts are updated.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: To practice this skill, when you make a decision, find nuances where a different decision would be better. Write out, “It depends. If X, then A is the best choice. If Y, then B is the best choice. I think this situation is X, so A.” While it's helpful to explore "it depends," only share that longer answer if it's actually helpful. You don't want to annoy your teammates.
